title: Peer-to-peer wallet
brief: People split dinner by sending each other money from their phones. A transfer takes money from one balance and adds it to another, and the sender must see the new balance right away. A flaky mobile connection often makes the app send the same transfer twice.

clarify.q: Can a balance ever be wrong, even for a second?
clarify.a: The sender must always see their own latest balance. Other people can wait a moment.

clarify.q: What if the phone loses signal after tapping Send?
clarify.a: The app retries with the same transfer key. The money must move once.

clarify.q: What does a regulator ask for?
clarify.a: A tamper-proof record of every transfer, encryption, and proof that every action was a signed-in user.

notes: Money is counted in cents, never in decimals.
Transfers settle between balances inside the wallet.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Transfers per day at 55 percent average load

hints: A reader may use a copy that is a moment behind. Which reads in this app must never do that?
Money lives in one strongly consistent store, with replication that waits for the copy (sync) so a failover loses nothing. A ledger database fits. Do not cache balances.
Uniqueness must be scoped to the business transfer, not the network attempt. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Two ideas carry the design. First, a transfer key (idempotency) turns a repeated tap into one transfer. Second, balances live in a strictly consistent ledger store, replicated in step across zones, with no cache in front. Push notifications are the only async part: they go through a queue because nobody is waiting for them.

designs.name: One strict ledger, keyed transfers
designs.why: Reads and transfers share the same strongly consistent store, so a sender always sees their latest balance. A failover loses nothing because the standby copy was written in step.

tradeoffs: No cache on balances means every balance read hits the ledger. It costs more database and avoids ever showing a stale balance after a transfer.
Sync replication adds a few milliseconds to each transfer and guarantees a failover loses nothing. Async would be faster and could drop the last second of transfers.
The transfer key is checked before the money moves. A tiny extra lookup stops a double tap on a bad connection from paying twice.
Notifications through a queue mean a push may arrive a second late, but a push outage can never block a transfer.
editorial.realWorld: Consumer wallets typically hold balances in a relational database and move money with a single transaction per transfer. A few thousand transfers a second is a large wallet (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A transfer is retried while another transfer spends the same balance. What transaction and uniqueness rule prevent double spending or creating money?
correctness.discussion: Give each transfer a stable unique id. In one transaction, check available funds, debit the sender, credit the receiver and save the transfer result. Lock the affected balances in a consistent order or use serializable isolation with retries. A duplicate transfer id returns the saved result. Keep immutable balanced ledger entries for audit; a separate debit followed by a credit can lose money after a crash. A pre-read alone cannot prevent double spending. The money-conservation invariant belongs inside one atomic commit. Uniqueness must be scoped to the business transfer, not the network attempt.

fields.label: Step 1. Balance is 10; two concurrent transfers each spend 8. What commits?
options: At most one after a serialized or locked funds check
fields.explanation: A pre-read alone cannot prevent double spending.

fields.label: Step 2. The process crashes between debit and credit. What should storage show?
options: A debit now and a reconciliation credit tomorrow
Both ledger sides and transfer id commit, or neither
fields.explanation: The money-conservation invariant belongs inside one atomic commit.

fields.label: Step 3. Transfer T is retried after losing its reply. What returns?
options: The durable result for T without another debit
A new transfer because its HTTP request is new
fields.explanation: Uniqueness must be scoped to the business transfer, not the network attempt.

correctness.responsibility: Conserve funds with atomic, unique transfers under concurrent spending.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
